.Swoosh 404.tagline: Site Takeover | Gamified Product Release | more

meta.v: Engineer · site takeover, game loop, rendering, leaderboard integration

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it exists
paras: A 404 page was the last surface anyone was going to fight over, which made it the right place to put a game. The shoe releasing was named 404 — the joke wrote itself, and the error page became campaign real estate.

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it matters
paras: It proved a small thing internally: play could ship on the same timeline as a product page. Six weeks, two people, no new platform. That argument opened doors for later work.

blocks.label: Process
blocks.title: Getting it to feel right
blocks.note: Most of the six weeks went into feel, not features.

items.title: Keyboard-first or touch-first
items.body: Traffic was 80% mobile, but the genre is a keyboard genre. Twin-stick controls on a phone felt terrible in the first build.

chose.v: One-axis drag with auto-fire. Your thumb only decides where, never when.

passed.v: A virtual joystick plus a fire button.

items.call: Removing the fire button removed the only thing testers complained about.

items.title: No score wall
items.body: A leaderboard was scoped, then cut two weeks in.

chose.v: A personal best held locally, surfaced only after your second run.

passed.v: A global leaderboard with member accounts.

items.call: The auth flow was longer than the game. Cutting it kept the whole thing a two-tap experience.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.title: End note
paras: The best decision was scoping it as a toy, not a product. Nothing in it needed to be maintained, so nothing in it needed to be negotiated.

index.summary: Marketing Event - Site takeover + gamified product release

Max's Lab.tagline: An explorable 3D world built around Max, with hidden details and live events.
Max's Lab.cover: Cover — 8s loop of the world at first load, camera settling

meta.v: Lead Front End engineer · 3D world, event system, performance budget
2 designers, 1 3D artist, 3 engineers, brand + product marketing

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it exists
paras: Air Max Day is an annual moment with a lot of noise around it. The brief was a destination that could hold a month of drops, unlocks, and live moments without becoming a landing page that gets rebuilt every week.
We built a room instead of a page: a single navigable 3D space where each object is a slot the marketing team can fill. New drop, new object. No redeploy, no new route.
blocks.pull: A page expires. A room gets furniture.

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it matters
paras: Members were arriving from social with no context and bouncing in under twenty seconds. A destination that rewards a second look changes the shape of that session — we needed exploration to be the thing that retains, not copy.
It also gave the team an authoring surface. Anything placed in the room could be scheduled, so a live event became a state change rather than a build.

blocks.label: Process
blocks.title: Building the room
blocks.note: Component-level captures from the middle of the build.

items.caption: Navigation prototype — camera rails vs. free orbit
Draw-call budget instrumentation on a mid-tier Android
Event scheduler preview in the CMS

items.title: Free orbit or camera rails
items.body: Free orbit tested as more fun for the first minute and worse for everything after — people got lost behind geometry and never found the drop.

chose.v: Rails with local look-around. Movement is constrained to authored paths; the camera can still pan inside each stop.

passed.v: Full orbit. It made every object a potential dead end and doubled the collision work.

items.call: Exploration only reads as exploration if you can always find your way back. Rails cost novelty and bought comprehension.

items.title: Hiding the drop behind interaction
items.body: Product marketing wanted the release visible on load. We wanted it earned — two taps in, behind a door.

chose.v: Earned placement, with a persistent pill that jumps you straight to the drop if you want the shortcut.

passed.v: A hero card on load. It answered the whole page in one glance.

items.call: The compromise held: the shortcut protected conversion, and the room still had a secret in it.

items.title: A hard 60fps floor on mid-tier Android
items.body: Frame rate was treated as a design constraint, not a QA pass. Everything past the budget had to justify itself against something already in the scene.

chose.v: One dynamic light, baked ambient occlusion, instanced props, and a dithered shadow catcher instead of real-time shadows.

items.call: The dither ended up defining the look of the whole thing. The constraint became the style.

blocks.label: Impact
blocks.title: What it moved
blocks.note: Measured over the 30-day campaign window against the prior year’s equivalent page.

items.note: vs. the previous Air Max Day page

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.title: What I’d do differently
paras: The authoring layer arrived late, so the first two events were hand-placed by engineers. If I ran it again the CMS schema would come before the geometry — the room only pays off if the team can furnish it without us.
I’d also cut a third of the props. The scene was legible at forty objects and busy at sixty, and we found that out after the shadow work.

index.summary: An explorable 3D world built around Max, with hidden details and live events.

EA Sports FC Partner Page.tagline: An interactive player viewer and reusable components for the EA Sports FC launch.
EA Sports FC Partner Page.cover: Cover — player viewer orbit, kit swap

meta.v: Engineer · player viewer, shared component work

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it exists
paras: A co-branded launch with a partner’s asset pipeline, a partner’s review cycle, and a fixed date. The interesting engineering problem was not the viewer — it was making the viewer out of parts that already existed.

items.title: Fork the viewer or extend the shared one
items.body: The shared 3D viewer did 80% of this. Extending it meant negotiating with two other teams’ roadmaps; forking meant shipping on time and owning a duplicate.

chose.v: Extended the shared viewer behind a feature flag, with the partner-specific material work isolated in an adapter.

passed.v: A fork. Faster that week, a tax every week after.

items.call: Two other launches used the adapter within a quarter. The negotiation paid for itself.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.title: End note
paras: Partner work is mostly interface design between organisations. The adapter boundary was the actual deliverable.

index.summary: An interactive player viewer and reusable components for the EA Sports FC launch.

Our Force 1 Poster Content Display Page.tagline: A collection story told through an authorable page, parallax, and animated 3D posters.
Our Force 1 Poster Content Display Page.cover: Cover — poster rotating through three collection panels

meta.v: Lead engineer · authoring model, scroll system, 3D poster pipeline

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it exists
paras: The collection had eleven chapters and no fixed length — chapters were still being written while we built. A hand-laid page would have been obsolete before launch.
So the deliverable was a grammar, not a layout: nine section types the editorial team could stack in any order, each with a defined scroll behaviour and a defined failure mode.
blocks.pull: The deliverable was a grammar, not a layout.

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it matters
paras: It shifted who owns the page. Editorial published three chapters after launch with no engineering involvement, which is the only real test of an authoring system.

blocks.label: Process
blocks.title: The section grammar
blocks.note: Each type had to survive being placed next to any other type.

items.title: Capping parallax depth
items.body: Design wanted more separation between layers. At the depth they wanted, text became unreadable mid-scroll on a trackpad.

chose.v: A depth ceiling per section type, with text layers pinned to zero parallax.

passed.v: Per-layer freehand depth in the CMS.

items.call: Type that moves while you read it is a bug wearing a costume. The ceiling was the compromise that let everything else stay loose.

items.title: Real 3D posters or pre-rendered loops
items.body: Eleven chapters × three posters is thirty-three assets. Live 3D meant a real engine on the page; pre-rendering meant a render farm and no interactivity.

chose.v: Live 3D for the hero poster, pre-rendered loops for the rest — one engine instance, thirty-two video textures.

items.call: One interactive poster per chapter was enough to sell the idea. The rest just had to move.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.title: End note
paras: The adjacency matrix was the highest-leverage artifact of the project and it was a spreadsheet. Constraints documented early are cheaper than constraints discovered in review.

index.summary: A collection story told through an authorable page, parallax, and animated 3D posters.

Moodie.tagline: An infinite discovery canvas for collecting and exploring visual inspiration.
Moodie.cover: Cover — canvas pan and zoom, boards resolving

meta.v: Solo, with a handful of very patient testers

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it exists
paras: My own reference collection had become four thousand screenshots in a folder. Every tool I tried made me file things, and filing is the step where collecting dies.
Moodie has no folders. Everything lands on one infinite canvas, and proximity is the only organising principle.
blocks.pull: Filing is the step where collecting dies.

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it matters
paras: It is the piece I use to test how far interaction can carry structure. If spatial memory can replace a taxonomy for four thousand items, that is worth knowing.

blocks.label: Process
blocks.title: Process assets
blocks.note: Mostly performance work disguised as interaction work.

items.caption: Tile virtualization at four zoom levels
Drop → thumbnail → placed, in one gesture

items.title: No search
items.body: The obvious feature. I have not built it, on purpose, for a year.

chose.v: Zoom-to-find. Getting somewhere is always a movement, never a query.

passed.v: Text search over tags and OCR.

items.call: Search would let me stop designing the canvas. Every time I have wanted it, the real problem was that zoom was too slow — and that was fixable.

items.title: Local-first with no account
items.body: No sync means no server, no auth, no privacy policy, and no access from a second machine.

chose.v: IndexedDB, with export to a single file.

items.call: The export file is the sync story until someone other than me needs it.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.title: Where it stands
paras: It holds my whole reference library and I have not opened the old folder in months, which is the only success metric I set.
The next problem is sharing a region without sharing the canvas. That probably requires the account I have been avoiding.

index.summary: An infinite discovery canvas for collecting and exploring visual inspiration.

Minecraft Clone.tagline: A multiplayer voxel world with procedural terrain and custom physics, built in React.

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it exists
paras: I wanted to understand chunked meshing and collision from the ground up rather than from a tutorial. Voxels are the cheapest way to be forced to learn both.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.title: End note
paras: The physics took four times longer than the rendering, which is the lesson.
